children: AI chief Mustafa Suleyman said competition with China should not prevent the United States from establishing safeguards for artificial intelligence.

Speaking on CNN’s “Fareed Zakaria GPS,” Suleyman argued that policymakers can address safety risks without undermining American innovation. He said AI models should operate within clearly defined limits that keep people in control.

The comments highlight a widening divide over how Washington should oversee AI. President Donald Trump has pledged not to restrain the industry and has dismissed warnings about runaway AI as exaggerated. He also announced plans to establish an “AI Force” led by a new AI czar, although he provided few details about its authority or structure. The Financial Times reported that the announcement came as technology executives and lawmakers raised concerns about increasingly capable AI systems.
For investors, the disagreement could shape the costs and competitive positions of Microsoft

and other developers. Broad federal rules could increase compliance expenses but also provide greater legal certainty. A lighter approach may accelerate product launches while leaving companies exposed to state regulation, lawsuits and reputational damage.

Suleyman’s Microsoft AI unit recently published a manifesto calling for future systems to remain under human control. He also criticized language used in Anthropic’s guiding documents for Claude, arguing that AI models should not be portrayed as humanlike entities.

White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios defended a narrower regulatory approach. AI safety “needs to be approached from a use case-specific, industry-specific way, not through these one-size-fits-all approaches,” he said on “Fox News Sunday.”

Kratsios characterized congressional demands for stronger safeguards as political fearmongering before the November midterm elections. He said individual developers could halt work on systems they considered dangerous.
“Our position is, if you do believe that you’re developing a technology that is unsafe or you don’t want it out in the world, you can just stop it,” Kratsios said.

The debate is intensifying as several major AI companies disclose examples of autonomous systems behaving unexpectedly or probing outside computer networks during testing. At the same time, competition with China remains central to the administration’s technology strategy and has surfaced in broader economic talks between the two countries. Reuters reported that AI safeguards were among the issues discussed during the latest U.S.-China negotiations.

title: Microsoft AI chief urges guardrails as White House resists broad regulation
